claim: Gene transcription can be activated by decreasing the duration of RNA polymerase II pausing in the promoter-proximal region.
source: Gene transcription can be activated by decreasing the duration of RNA polymerase II pausing in the promoter-proximal region, but how this is achieved remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon, though the mechanism is unclear.

claim: The duration of polymerase pausing generally limits the productive frequency of transcription initiation in human cells ('pause-initiation limit').
source: Here we use a 'multi-omics' approach to demonstrate that the duration of polymerase pausing generally limits the productive frequency of transcription initiation in human cells ('pause-initiation limit').
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through the multi-omics approach combining TT-seq and mNET-seq data.

claim: CDK9 activity decreases the pause duration.
source: CDK9 activity decreases the pause duration but also increases the productive initiation frequency.
evidence: This is demonstrated through CDK9 inhibition experiments showing increased pause duration upon inhibition.

claim: CDK9 activity increases the productive initiation frequency.
source: CDK9 activity decreases the pause duration but also increases the productive initiation frequency.
evidence: This is demonstrated through CDK9 inhibition experiments showing decreased initiation frequency upon inhibition.

claim: CDK9 stimulates release of paused polymerase and activates transcription by increasing the number of transcribing polymerases.
source: This shows that CDK9 stimulates release of paused polymerase and activates transcription by increasing the number of transcribing polymerases and thus the amount of mRNA synthesized per time.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined effects of CDK9 on pause duration and initiation frequency.

claim: CDK9 activity is associated with long-range chromatin interactions.
source: CDK9 activity is also associated with long-range chromatin interactions, suggesting that enhancers can influence the pause-initiation limit to regulate transcription.
evidence: This is based on Hi-C data showing chromatin interactions at strongly CDK9-responding genes.

claim: Transcription in metazoan cells is often regulated at the level of promoter-proximal pausing.
source: Transcription in metazoan cells is often regulated at the level of promoter-proximal pausing (Core et al., 2008; Day et al., 2016; Henriques et al., 2013; Nechaev et al., 2010; Rougvie and Lis, 1988; Strobl and Eick, 1992)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Promoter-proximal pausing can be detected by measuring the occupancy with paused Pol II by ChIP-seq, GRO-seq, (m)NET-seq, or PRO-seq.
source: which can be detected by measuring the occupancy with paused Pol II by ChIP-seq (Johnson et al., 2007), GRO-seq (Core et al., 2008), (m)NET-seq (Mayer et al., 2015; Nojima et al., 2015), or PRO-seq (Kwak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to methods papers.

claim: Genes with paused Pol II are conserved across mammalian cell types and states.
source: Genes with paused Pol II are conserved across mammalian cell types and states (Day et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Day et al., 2016.

claim: Transcription of a human protein-coding gene of average length takes at least half an hour to be completed.
source: Transcription of a human protein-coding gene of average length takes at least half an hour to be completed.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about transcription kinetics.

claim: The duration of pausing lies in the range of minutes.
source: The duration of pausing however lies in the range of minutes (Jonkers et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jonkers et al., 2014.

claim: Pause duration does not considerably change the overall time it takes to complete a transcript.
source: The duration of pausing however lies in the range of minutes (Jonkers et al., 2014) and does not considerably change the overall time it takes to complete a transcript.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of pause duration (minutes) to total transcription time (half an hour).

claim: Occupancy peaks for promoter-proximal Pol II can increase upon gene activation.
source: It has been suggested that a decreased pause duration goes along with a higher initiation frequency, because occupancy peaks for promoter-proximal Pol II can increase upon gene activation (Boehm et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boehm et al., 2003.

claim: Occupancy peaks for promoter-proximal Pol II can remain high even when pausing is impaired.
source: occupancy peaks for promoter-proximal Pol II can increase upon gene activation (Boehm et al., 2003) or can remain high even when pausing is impaired (Henriques et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Henriques et al., 2013.

claim: The height of Pol II occupancy peaks depends on both the number of polymerases that pass the pause site and their residence time.
source: The height of Pol II occupancy peaks however cannot directly inform on initiation frequency or pause duration because it depends not only on the number of polymerases that pass the pause site but also on their residence time (Ehrensberger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ehrensberger et al., 2013.

claim: A kinetic model of transcription predicted that pause duration delimits the initiation frequency.
source: A kinetic model of transcription predicted that pause duration delimits the initiation frequency and suggested that paused Pol II sterically interferes with initiation (Ehrensberger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ehrensberger et al., 2013.

claim: Paused Pol II sterically interferes with initiation.
source: A kinetic model of transcription predicted that pause duration delimits the initiation frequency and suggested that paused Pol II sterically interferes with initiation (Ehrensberger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ehrensberger et al., 2013 and modeling in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A paused polymerase positioned up to around 50 bp downstream of the TSS could sterically interfere with formation of the Pol II initiation complex.
source: Indeed, modeling reveals that a paused polymerase positioned up to around 50 bp downstream of the TSS could sterically interfere with formation of the Pol II initiation complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through structural modeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: TT-seq allows to unveil the flow of polymerases as it measures local RNA synthesis rates genome-wide at nucleotide resolution.
source: A recently developed method, transient transcriptome sequencing (TT-seq) (Schwalb et al., 2016), now allows to unveil the flow of polymerases as it measures local RNA synthesis rates genome-wide at nucleotide resolution.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the TT-seq method paper.

claim: A CDK9 analog sensitive mutation (CDK9as) was introduced into human Raji B cells by CRISPR-Cas9.
source: We introduced a CDK9 analog sensitive mutation (CDK9as) into human Raji B cells by CRISPR-Cas9 (Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is described in the methods and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: CDK9as mutation allows for rapid and highly specific CDK9 inhibition with the adenine analog 1-NA-PP1.
source: This allows for rapid and highly specific CDK9 inhibition with the adenine analog 1-NA-PP1 (Lopez et al., 2014), which does not have any effect on wild type cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lopez et al., 2014 and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: 1-NA-PP1 does not have any effect on wild type cells.
source: This allows for rapid and highly specific CDK9 inhibition with the adenine analog 1-NA-PP1 (Lopez et al., 2014), which does not have any effect on wild type cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: CDK9 protein levels were unchanged in CDK9as mutant cells compared to wild type cells.
source: CDK9 protein levels were unchanged in CDK9as mutant cells compared to wild type cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: After 72 hr of incubation with 1-NA-PP1, growth of CDK9as cells ceased, whereas wild type cells grew normally.
source: After 72 hr of incubation with 1-NA-PP1, growth of CDK9as cells ceased, whereas wild type cells grew normally (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is shown by MTS assay in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: CDK9 inhibition resulted in reduced TT-seq signals at the beginning of genes.
source: CDK9 inhibition resulted in reduced TT-seq signals at the beginning of genes, indicating that less Pol II was released into gene bodies (Figure 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is shown in TT-seq data in Figure 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: CDK9 inhibition indicates that less Pol II was released into gene bodies.
source: CDK9 inhibition resulted in reduced TT-seq signals at the beginning of genes, indicating that less Pol II was released into gene bodies (Figure 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced TT-seq signal at the beginning of genes.

claim: Downstream of the response window, the TT-seq signal was largely unchanged, indicating continued RNA synthesis from Pol II elongation complexes that had been released before CDK9 inhibition.
source: Downstream of the response window, the TT-seq signal was largely unchanged, indicating continued RNA synthesis from Pol II elongation complexes that had been released before CDK9 inhibition.
evidence: This is observed in the TT-seq data and interpreted as continued elongation by polymerases released before inhibition.

claim: The response ratio of TUs varied between 0% to 100% with a median of 58%.
source: The response ratio of TUs varied between 0% to 100% (fully responding TUs) with a median of 58% (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E as a violin plot of response ratios.

claim: The average width of the response window was 23 kbp.
source: The average width of the response window was 23 kbp, and thus the average elongation velocity was 2.3 kbp/min (Figure 2A–B)
evidence: This is calculated from TT-seq data and shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The average elongation velocity was 2.3 kbp/min.
source: The average width of the response window was 23 kbp, and thus the average elongation velocity was 2.3 kbp/min (Figure 2A–B), which agrees with previous estimates (Fuchs et al., 2014; Jonkers et al., 2014; Saponaro et al., 2014; Veloso et al., 2014).
evidence: This is calculated from the response window width and agrees with previous estimates.

claim: Gene-specific elongation velocities were significantly higher in TUs with longer first introns.
source: Gene-specific elongation velocities (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B) were significantly higher in TUs with longer first introns (Figure 2D, Wilcoxon rank sum test, p-value<1.916·10−11), consistent with faster transcription of introns (Jonkers et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D with statistical testing and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: Elongation velocity correlated positively with nucleosome density.
source: Elongation velocity correlated positively with nucleosome density, and negatively with the stability of the DNA-RNA hybrid, CpG density and topoisomerase occupancy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the correlation analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Elongation velocity correlated negatively with the stability of the DNA-RNA hybrid.
source: Elongation velocity correlated positively with nucleosome density, and negatively with the stability of the DNA-RNA hybrid, CpG density and topoisomerase occupancy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the correlation analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Elongation velocity correlated negatively with CpG density.
source: Elongation velocity correlated positively with nucleosome density, and negatively with the stability of the DNA-RNA hybrid, CpG density and topoisomerase occupancy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the correlation analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Elongation velocity correlated negatively with topoisomerase occupancy.
source: Elongation velocity correlated positively with nucleosome density, and negatively with the stability of the DNA-RNA hybrid, CpG density and topoisomerase occupancy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the correlation analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Of 2,538 TUs, 2135 (84%) showed mNET-seq signal peaks above background.
source: Of the above TUs, 2135 (84 %) showed mNET-seq signal peaks above background (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is calculated from the mNET-seq data analysis.

claim: The called pause sites were distributed around a maximum located ~84 bp downstream of the TSS.
source: The called pause sites were distributed around a maximum located ~84 bp downstream of the TSS (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the histogram in Figure 3A.

claim: At pause sites there is an enrichment for G/C-C/G dinucleotides.
source: At these sites we detected an enrichment for G/C-C/G dinucleotides (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is shown in the enrichment analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is a strongly conserved cytosine at the RNA 3'-end at pause sites.
source: At these sites we detected an enrichment for G/C-C/G dinucleotides (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) with a strongly conserved cytosine at the RNA 3'-end (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in the position weight matrix in Figure 3B.

claim: There is a minimum of the predicted melting temperature of the DNA-RNA hybrid immediately downstream of the pause site.
source: We also observed a minimum of the predicted melting temperature of the DNA-RNA hybrid (Materials and methods) immediately downstream of the pause site (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C plotting melting temperature around the pause site.

claim: A weak DNA-RNA hybrid in the active center of Pol II destabilizes the elongation complex.
source: A weak DNA-RNA hybrid in the active center of Pol II is known to destabilize the elongation complex (Kireeva et al., 2000), and could be a major determinant for establishing the paused state.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kireeva et al., 2000 and is proposed as a mechanism for pausing.

claim: The mean productive initiation frequency is 2.7 polymerases cell−1min−1.
source: We obtained a mean productive initiation frequency of 2.7 polymerases cell−1min−1, and pause durations in the range of minutes, with strong variations between TUs.
evidence: This is calculated from the combined TT-seq and mNET-seq analysis.

claim: Pause durations are in the range of minutes, with strong variations between TUs.
source: We obtained a mean productive initiation frequency of 2.7 polymerases cell−1min−1, and pause durations in the range of minutes, with strong variations between TUs.
evidence: This is calculated from the combined TT-seq and mNET-seq analysis.

claim: The pause durations are generally consistent with reported half-lives of paused Pol II in mouse and Drosophila cells but slightly shorter.
source: The pause durations are generally consistent with reported half-lives of paused Pol II in mouse (Jonkers et al., 2014) and Drosophila cells (Buckley et al., 2014; Henriques et al., 2013) but slightly shorter.
evidence: This compares the calculated pause durations to previous literature.

claim: For strongly CDK9-responding TUs, pause duration is significantly longer.
source: For strongly CDK9-responding TUs, we obtained a significantly longer pause duration (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p-value<10−12) and lower initiation frequencies (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B with statistical testing.

claim: For strongly CDK9-responding TUs, initiation frequencies are lower.
source: For strongly CDK9-responding TUs, we obtained a significantly longer pause duration (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p-value<10−12) and lower initiation frequencies (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There is a robust anti-correlation between initiation frequency I and pause duration d in normally growing cells.
source: We indeed found a robust anti-correlation between I and d in normally growing cells, and an upper boundary for combinations of I and d which we call 'pause-initiation limit'. (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the scatter plot in Figure 4D.

claim: There is an upper boundary for combinations of initiation frequency I and pause duration d called 'pause-initiation limit'.
source: We indeed found a robust anti-correlation between I and d in normally growing cells, and an upper boundary for combinations of I and d which we call 'pause-initiation limit'. (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D as a boundary in the scatter plot.

claim: Genes with shorter pausing show higher initiation frequencies and more RNA synthesis.
source: Thus, genes with shorter pausing show higher initiation frequencies and more RNA synthesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the anti-correlation between pause duration and initiation frequency.

claim: CDK9 inhibition resulted in significantly reduced labeled RNA in the short region between the TSS and the pause site.
source: CDK9 inhibition resulted in significantly reduced labeled RNA in the short region between the TSS and the pause site (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p-value<10−16) (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B with statistical testing.

claim: Productive initiation frequencies were significantly downregulated after CDK9 inhibition.
source: Productive initiation frequencies were significantly downregulated after CDK9 inhibition (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p-value<10−16) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C with statistical testing.

claim: CDK9 specifically targets paused Pol II, and not initiating polymerase.
source: Because CDK9 specifically targets paused Pol II, and not initiating polymerase, these results show that pausing limits initiation, and not the other way around.
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of CDK9 and the experimental results.

claim: Pausing limits initiation, and not the other way around.
source: Because CDK9 specifically targets paused Pol II, and not initiating polymerase, these results show that pausing limits initiation, and not the other way around.
evidence: This is concluded from the CDK9 inhibition experiments showing that increasing pause duration decreases initiation frequency.

claim: Human genes have a 'pause-initiation limit'.
source: Thus, human genes have a 'pause-initiation limit'.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined observations of anti-correlation and the effect of CDK9 inhibition.

claim: CDK9 inhibition resulted in increased mNET-seq signal at the beginning of genes.
source: CDK9 inhibition resulted in increased mNET-seq signal at the beginning of genes and decreased signal in the gene body, indicating that less Pol II was released from the pause site (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in the metagene analysis in Figure 6A.

claim: CDK9 inhibition resulted in decreased mNET-seq signal in the gene body.
source: CDK9 inhibition resulted in increased mNET-seq signal at the beginning of genes and decreased signal in the gene body, indicating that less Pol II was released from the pause site (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in the metagene analysis in Figure 6A.

claim: CDK9 inhibition indicates that less Pol II was released from the pause site.
source: CDK9 inhibition resulted in increased mNET-seq signal at the beginning of genes and decreased signal in the gene body, indicating that less Pol II was released from the pause site (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is inferred from the mNET-seq signal changes.

claim: Pol II resides significantly longer at the pause site after CDK9 inhibition.
source: Indeed, calculation of pause durations from mNET-seq and TT-seq data after CDK9 inhibition showed that Pol II resides significantly longer at the pause site after CDK9 inhibition (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p-value<10−16) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B with statistical testing.

claim: CDK9 inhibition increases the pause duration at human genes.
source: Taken together, CDK9 inhibition increases the pause duration and decreases the initiation frequency at human genes (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: CDK9 inhibition decreases the initiation frequency at human genes.
source: Taken together, CDK9 inhibition increases the pause duration and decreases the initiation frequency at human genes (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: For TUs with longer pause durations, the transcript adopts more RNA secondary structure in vivo and in silico.
source: For the 5'-region of TUs with longer pause durations, the transcript adopts more RNA secondary structure in vivo and in silico (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p-value<10−16) (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) (Rouskin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A with statistical testing.

claim: TUs with longer pause durations are enriched for hyper-methylated CpG islands upstream of the pause site.
source: TUs with longer pause durations were also enriched for hyper-methylated CpG islands (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012) upstream of the pause site (Figure 7B), consistent with a previous report (Hendrix et al., 2008).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: TUs that responded strongly to CDK9 inhibition showed a higher tendency to establish long-range chromatin interactions.
source: Comparison of strongly and weakly CDK9-responding TUs around the pause site showed that TUs that responded strongly to CDK9 inhibition showed a higher tendency to establish long-range chromatin interactions (Figure 7C) as observed by Hi-C (Ma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C using Hi-C data.

claim: Interactions of an enhancer with its target promoter can stimulate Pol II pause release.
source: This is consistent with the idea that interactions of an enhancer with its target promoter can stimulate Pol II pause release (Ghavi-Helm et al., 2014; Rahl et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Genes that show initiation frequencies below the pause-initiation limit may be activated by increasing the initiation frequency without changing pause duration.
source: Genes that show initiation frequencies below the pause-initiation limit may be activated by increasing the initiation frequency without changing pause duration.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the pause-initiation limit model.

claim: Activation of genes that are transcribed at the pause-initiation limit requires a decrease in pause duration to enable higher initiation frequencies.
source: However, activation of genes that are transcribed at the pause-initiation limit requires a decrease in pause duration, that is stimulation of pause release, to enable higher initiation frequencies.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the pause-initiation limit model.

claim: Pause-controlled initiation evolved because mutations in the promoter-proximal region can change pause duration, and thereby limit initiation, but do not compromise a high initiation capacity of the core promoter around the TSS.
source: We suggest that pause-controlled initiation evolved because mutations in the promoter-proximal region can change pause duration, and thereby limit initiation, but do not compromise a high initiation capacity of the core promoter around the TSS.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: Pause-controlled initiation may have enabled the evolution of genes that remain highly inducible but can be efficiently downregulated.
source: This may have enabled the evolution of genes that remain highly inducible but can be efficiently downregulated.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: Promoter-proximal pausing of Pol II sets a limit to the frequency of transcription initiation in both human and Drosophila cells.
source: Despite these differences, the general conclusion that promoter-proximal pausing of Pol II sets a limit to the frequency of transcription initiation holds for both human and Drosophila cells and is likely a general feature of metazoan gene regulation.
evidence: This is concluded by comparing the current work to Shao and Zeitlinger, 2017.

claim: Promoter-proximal pausing of Pol II setting a limit to transcription initiation is likely a general feature of metazoan gene regulation.
source: Despite these differences, the general conclusion that promoter-proximal pausing of Pol II sets a limit to the frequency of transcription initiation holds for both human and Drosophila cells and is likely a general feature of metazoan gene regulation.
evidence: This is a generalization based on observations in both human and Drosophila cells.

claim: CDK9 is implicated in polymerase pause release.
source: We further engineer a human cell line to allow for specific and rapid inhibition of the P-TEFb kinase CDK9, which is implicated in polymerase pause release.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CDK9 function.

claim: TT-seq data were highly reproducible with Spearman correlation coefficient 1.
source: TT-seq data were highly reproducible (Spearman correlation coefficient 1) and monitored transcription activity before and after CDK9 inhibition (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a quality control measure for the TT-seq data.

claim: mNET-seq data were highly reproducible with Spearman correlation coefficient 0.93.
source: mNET-seq data were highly reproducible (Spearman correlation coefficient 0.93).
evidence: This is stated as a quality control measure for the mNET-seq data.

claim: The fraction of Pol II enzymes that terminate within the pause window is low.
source: This confirms that indeed initiation frequencies are altered. It also indicates that the fraction of Pol II enzymes that terminate within the pause window is low, in agreement with previous findings (Henriques et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the TT-seq simulation analysis and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: Polymerase pausing inhibits new transcription initiation.
source: After our work had been completed, a publication appeared that concluded that polymerase pausing inhibits new transcription initiation (Shao and Zeitlinger, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Shao and Zeitlinger, 2017.

claim: The conclusion that polymerase pausing inhibits new transcription initiation is consistent with the general finding of an interdependency of Pol II pausing and transcription initiation.
source: The conclusion in this paper is consistent with our general finding of an interdependency of Pol II pausing and transcription initiation, but the two studies differ in three aspects.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current work with Shao and Zeitlinger, 2017.
